Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Objective of the Game In Kelp, one player takes the role of the Shark, trying to hunt the Octopus, and the other takes the role of the Octopus, trying to survive. Both players have different goals and paths to victory. The Octopus wins either by surviving until the Shark is exhausted, or by eating all four food blocks. The Shark has only one way to win: by successfully striking the Octopus and beating it in the final confrontation. Anatomy of the Board The board represents a Kelp forest and is divided into different zones. Zones The Exposed Zone is in the center. The Kelp Zones are adjacent to it. The Rocky Zones are in the corners of the board. Shark Den The Rocky Zones include the Shark Dens. On one of these Current spaces the Shark starts the game, and it may also be returned there because of certain in-game actions. Block Space Each zone has a space for the Octopus blocks. Zone Value Each zone has a value that represents the visibility in that part of the Kelp forest. The Exposed Zone has value 2+, the Kelp Zones 4+, and so on - a placed die must be equal to or greater than the zone value. Shark Movement Path The lines represent the path the Shark can follow when it moves. Current Space The blue squares represent Current spaces. The Shark moves on these spaces and can place Current dice on them. Food Track Food blocks are placed here whenever the Octopus eats them. Hunger Track Dice are placed here whenever the Shark uses stored Energy or strikes. Growth Track Formed by the 4 Growth tiles; grants the Shark permanent abilities. Setup This is automated on BGA, but for better understanding see as follows: Fill the Shark dice bag with 7 blue Currents dice, 3 yellow Search dice, and 1 red Strike die (as indicated on the Shark's player aid). Place the remaining dice within reach of the Shark to form the supply. Shuffle the Shark deck, deal 4 cards face-up to the designated row, and place the rest of the deck face-down in the space to its left. Place the 4 Growth tiles with the sides showing the spaces for the dice face-up, in the corresponding numbered slots. From the Octopus cards, remove all starter cards with the special starter symbols and set them aside. Separate the remaining Octopus cards by color and form 4 piles: Learn (blue), Eat (orange), Hide (purple), and Move (yellow). Shuffle each pile individually and place it face-up on the Octopus player's side of the table. Place the matching food block on the top Eat card. Place the other 3 food blocks, 1 shell, 1 double shell, and the 3 traps next to the card piles. Place the hand size token with the number 4 facing up on the space above the draw pile. Place the 3 Shark and 3 Octopus confrontation cards face-down next to the board. Put the remaining 9 blocks (1 Octopus, 1 trap, and 7 shells) into the Octopus bag. The Octopus shuffles the blocks in the bag and draws them one at a time, placing them standing upright in the block spaces (from top to bottom, left to right). Only the Octopus should see the block symbols. Once all blocks are placed, put the bag to the side. Take the card Fast Learning and set it aside. Shuffle the remaining starter cards and place them face-down to form the draw pile. The Octopus takes the starting card Fast Learning and draws 3 additional cards from the starting deck to form the opening hand. The Octopus places the Shark on 1 of the 4 dens, on a Current space, pointing at the center of the board. The game begins. The Octopus takes the first turn. The Octopus As the Octopus, you play cards that let you move stealthily and manipulate the position of the blocks on the board. Most cards come at the cost of revealing blocks, but some cards let you hide them again. Your goal is to survive - win by outlasting the Shark until it is exhausted, or by feasting on all 4 food blocks. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Ok gameplay during beginning and middle.  End is so dumb with rock paper scissors deciding the victor.  Needs ending completely reworked. Edit:  So many paid reviews here.  People giving it 10s when they don't even have it.  Designer has an army of people leaving fake reviews and attacking people who leave bad reviews or try to resell their copies.  Shame on them!

[Rating: 1/10] I feel let down by the game, I backed it because I loved the theme and the mechanics seemed really fun to me. Unfortunately I didn't realise the final showdown essentially comes down to a 1 in 3 rock paper scissors style of determining the winner. I absolutely hate such a strategic game essentially coming down to random chance, it makes going through the rest of the game feel like a waste of time. I voiced my opinions on the Kickstarter and I fortunately the creator got really defensive rather than take on my comments, and now I can see lots of other people are having the same issue with the g

[Rating: 1/10] Looked intriguing at first as a hidden-movement game. But then learning the rules, and there's deck-building for the octopus, and dice-bag-building for the shark. There's tedious dice rolling just to determine what the shark can do. And then even when it finds the octopus, you play a rock-paper-scissors game to decide if it's over! Both sides have to build up their engines to get better cards and abilities, and..... so much of this is focused away from hidden-movement!  By the end I was the octopus who had almost nothing hidden. Not because of the stealth game, but because I had to flip tiles 

[Rating: 2/10] I'm just humiliatingly bad at hidden movement games. I felt very constrained in my options... also, I have my usual complaint about a deckbuilding game that doesn't allow me to deckbuild as much as I can in Dominion.

[Rating: 3/10] Der Oktopus muss nur Futter entwickeln und schnell fressen. Nichts anderes. Dann ist das Spiel ganz schnell vorbei. Die Regel sollte da wohl angepasst werden um wieder ein Spiel zu haben. So kann es nicht gemeint sein. Schade. Das Material und die Idee sind schon gut.

[Rating: 3/10] First game ended in 10 minutes due to randomness of tile shuffle, dice rolling, and 1/3 card flip. To me, that is not great design.  Second game shark player rolled two 6s which enabled them on their FIRST turn (thanks to random roll and random market)  bought the 10pt Hostile card. This card trashes 1/3 is the rock paper scissors card, making the win condition for the shart on hit a 50/50 shot.  No thank you

[Rating: 3/10] Bisher empfanden meine Haie das Spiel als wenig intuitiv: Und wenn man sich anschaut, dass das offizielle Regelvideo von Wonderbow rund zehnmal durch Einblendungen korrigiert werden musste (peinlich!), wird da wohl was dran sein.   Wenn man schlecht spielt, kann man leicht in eine Art "Endlosschleife" geraten, welche dazu führt, dass man das Spiel vor dem offiziellen Ende abbrechen muss, da es dem Hai nicht mehr möglich ist, zu gewinnen. Dies fühlt sich für beide Parteien in hohem Maße unbefriedigend an.   Das Deck-Building beim Oktopus macht leider nur wenig Spaß.

[Rating: 3/10] Trotz des enormen Hypes und der hohen Erwartungen, die durch die Kickstarter-Kampagne und die aufwendige Präsentation geschürt wurden, bleibt Kelp spielmechanisch blass. Die Balance zwischen Bluff, Taktik und Glück überzeugt nicht, und das Spielgefühl bleibt flach. Für mich reicht es daher nur für 3/10 Punkte – Kelp wandert wieder in die Bucht.

[Rating: 3/10] There is little more annoying in a board game than spending almost an hour playing a game to have the entire result come down to a coin flip. I could have just flipped a coin an hour ago and saved all that time.
